A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MedRegA research. Their main text, figures, tables, mathematical material, and Appendices A–E are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated content.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on medical VQA, report generation, classification, regional identification and detection, and Regional CoT, with quantitative results and generated examples.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds original annotation validation, paired bilingual evaluations, ReXrank results, and experiments adapting baseline models to regional tasks.

M1.justification: The InternVL 1.2 backbone, bounding-box encoding, two-stage training, language-model objective, and Regional CoT procedure are unchanged. The backbone components newly named in Section 4 were already specified in v1 Appendix B.1.

E1.justification: Appendix C.1.2 adds cross-language report-generation scenarios: Chinese reports for IU-Xray images and English reports for in-house images. These extend language/task pairings within existing medical coverage. ReXrank evaluates the already represented MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray datasets.

E2.justification: The new ReXrank comparison includes MedVersa, RGRG, RaDialog, and CheXagent alongside RadFM and BioMedGPT (v3 Table 9). Table 13 also introduces five-shot Med-Flamingo and fine-tuned LLaVA-Med as regional-task comparators. These substantially broaden the comparisons beyond the retained original baseline evaluations.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a 50-sample audit by two experts, two GPT-4o-translated bilingual sets of 100 samples each, and a 5K-sample regional subset using five-shot Med-Flamingo and ten-epoch LLaVA-Med fine-tuning. ReXrank adds an official benchmark protocol with RadCliQ-v0/v1 and SembScore. Existing experiments retain their reported settings.

E4.justification: v3 adds annotation-quality validation, language-transfer sensitivity tests and examples, and an experiment testing whether MedRegInstruct benefits other models. Figure 19 adds qualitative Regional CoT ablations for diagnosis and VQA. The original quantitative CoT ablation remains unchanged, moving from Table 11 to Table 14.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new human audit reports point accuracies without uncertainty estimates; its sample and annotator counts describe evaluation design rather than repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: All original numerical tables retain their results, allowing for renumbering and equivalent decimal formatting. Substantial additions include ReXrank and adapted-baseline results, annotation accuracies of 93.33% for report refinement and 72% for boxes, and paired-language results. For example, v3 Table 10 reports BLEU-1 of 48.99 in original English versus 10.04 in Chinese on the paired IU-Xray subset. These are new evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The bounding-box representation and Region-Aligned evaluation mathematics, including Hungarian matching, the IoU threshold, and Algorithm 1, are unchanged. No new formal assumptions, proofs, or derivations are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about MedRegInstruct, bilingual generalist MedRegA, three regional tasks, Regional CoT, and strong performance across eight modalities. The additional evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v3 attributes cross-language performance losses primarily to writing-style differences and argues that semantics are less affected (Appendix C.1.2). It also argues that somewhat oversized annotation boxes suffice for localization and interprets baseline adaptation as evidence of dataset utility. These add targeted explanations and applicability qualifications without replacing the original interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly identifies Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hospital as the clinical source and states that only constructed data derived from public datasets will be released. It documents GPT-4o translation and adaptation settings for the new experiments. Existing model-training details, hardware, and task prompts remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to ReXrank and Tanida et al.’s RGRG, plus discussion positioning MedRegA against specialist report generators and MedVersa. The dedicated related-work section and principal novelty positioning remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the overall section structure are retained. Changes include local wording edits, removal of a duplicated split-description sentence, additional report-evaluation paragraph headings, a new Appendix C.3, acknowledgements, expanded ethics text, and the conference-publication header.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the experimental displays with ReXrank, bilingual, and adapted-baseline tables (Tables 9, 10, and 13), plus bilingual examples, diagnosis examples, and qualitative CoT ablations (Figures 15, 16, and 19). Existing displays are retained and reflowed; v1 Tables 9–11 become Tables 11, 12, and 14, and Figures 15–16 become Figures 17–18.

improvement.justification: v1 provided no reported human validation of its automatic annotations and largely compared regional abilities against unadapted baselines. v3 directly investigates both gaps through expert validation and baseline adaptation. Its stronger report-generation comparisons and paired-language tests also better establish competitive standing and expose a previously untested generalization weakness. These substantially strengthen validation of the central contributions, although small validation sets, unequal training budgets, and the unverified style-based explanation leave limitations.
